name: The Great White Oak of Logan (Logan Oak)

location.address: Old Logan Cemetery, northeast corner, near the junction of Keynes Drive and North Mulberry Street, Logan, OH
location.neighbourhood: North side of Logan, Hocking County

access: Free, on the grounds of a public cemetery (Old Logan Cemetery); described by a visiting naturalist as easy to find, with respectful visitors welcome.
transport: No public transit found; car access in Logan, OH (Hocking County). Not close to any of our published US cities; treat as its own place (Logan, OH), roughly an hour southeast of Columbus.
story:
Logan sells this tree's children. The town's Tree Commission gathers acorns from underneath it, raises them into saplings and sells them as a fundraiser, which is a fairly literal way of keeping a tree going.

The parent is a white oak on the northeast corner of Old Logan Cemetery, put at roughly six hundred years, with a defensible range of five hundred to six hundred and fifty. Ohio's Department of Natural Resources checked the age about thirty years ago and nobody wrote down how, so treat that figure as a good estimate rather than a count of rings. Either way, it was standing here well before any European reached the Ohio valley.

What people come for is the shape. An Ohio naturalist spent an hour photographing it from every angle in 2019 and called it easily the largest and most ornate white oak he had seen: huge gnarled limbs leaving the trunk sideways rather than upward, the frame an oak only builds when it has room and several centuries. Its least likely honour came in 2022, when it turned up as an answer on College Jeopardy.

Nobody appears to have put a tape around it. If you have, tell us.

best_time.label: September and October, when the acorns drop and the town collects them

name: The Devil's Tree

location.address: Mountain Road, Martinsville section of Bernards Township, Somerset County, NJ

access: Stands alone in an undeveloped field the township has designated as a public open space with posted opening hours (closes about half an hour after sunset per an on-site sign, since 2007). The field itself may be entered without asking anyone's permission, but the tree's own trunk is ringed by a chain-link fence, installed after repeated vandalism and midnight visits, so it is view-only rather than touchable up close.
transport: No public transit found; car access off Mountain Road, Martinsville, NJ. Not close to any of our published US cities (nearest large city is Newark/NYC area, well over an hour); treat as its own place (Bernards Township / Martinsville, NJ).
story:
People have tried to cut this oak down with axes and with chainsaws, and it is still standing, carrying the marks. That is the part of the Devil's Tree that is not folklore.

The rest is. New Jersey tells a set of stories about it: that a car parked nearby will not start again, that the trunk stays warm in cold weather, that visitors go home with scratches nobody gave them. One local outlet has called it the most haunted place in the state. The stories are widely told, long-standing and unverified, and they are why most people come.

What they find is a single oak alone in an open field off Mountain Road, ringed by a chain-link fence the township put up after years of vandalism and night-time visits. The field is public open space and a sign gives the hours, closing about half an hour after sunset, which is presumably aimed at the visitors who made the fence necessary.

It is at least two hundred years old. No botanical survey has recorded which oak it is, so the species on this page reads simply as Quercus. If you know the answer from the leaves or the bark, we would like to hear it.

One clarification, because the two are confused constantly: this is not the Basking Ridge oak, the 600 year old white oak a few miles away that died in 2016 and was taken down the next year. This one is alive.

name: The Survivor Tree

location.address: Outdoor Symbolic Memorial, Oklahoma City National Memorial, 620 N Harvey Ave, Oklahoma City, Oklahoma

access: Free. The Outdoor Symbolic Memorial (which includes the Survivor Tree, the Gates of Time, the Field of Empty Chairs) is open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at no charge. Only the separate indoor Museum charges admission.
transport: Downtown Oklahoma City, already one of our published cities; the tree stands within the city itself.
story:
After the bombing, officials nearly took the tree down. The blast had driven glass and debris into its trunk, and the trunk was evidence.

The elm stood in the car park across the street from the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, and it had stood there long before the building did. Photographs from the 1920s, when the ground was the back yard of a family home, show it already growing, which puts it at around a hundred years old. On 19 April 1995 the explosion stripped away most of its branches.

It was left standing. About a year later it came into bloom again, and it was kept, as the centre of the outdoor grounds of the Oklahoma City National Memorial, on the north side of the site above the Field of Empty Chairs. The Rescuers' Orchard of redbuds, maples and elms was planted around it.

It is tended now more closely than most trees anywhere. Seed is collected from it and grown on, and the seedlings go to visitors and to partner sites elsewhere in the country, so the tree exists in more places than this one.

The outdoor memorial, the tree included, is open every hour of every day of the year and costs nothing. Only the indoor museum charges admission.

name: The Kalaloch Redcedar

location.address: Olympic National Park, off US Highway 101 between Ruby Beach and Kalaloch, Washington
location.neighbourhood: Kalaloch Big Cedar Nature Trail, a short flat walk from a signed roadside parking area

access: Free (within Olympic National Park); short, flat, well-marked trail a few hundred feet from a roadside parking pull-off on Highway 101. The access road has potholes but is passable by any vehicle.
transport: No public transit; nearest services are at Kalaloch Lodge, a few miles south.
story:
Half of this tree is lying on the ground. On 8 March 2014 a storm off the Pacific split the Kalaloch cedar down its length and roughly half the trunk and crown came down. The other half is still standing, and still alive.

That changes what to expect. The figures this tree is famous for, close to six metres through and about fifty three metres tall, are pre-2014 numbers from when it ranked among the largest western red cedars anywhere. Nobody has published a remeasurement since. What you walk up to now is a ruined column of a tree, somewhere between eight hundred and twelve hundred years old, described by everyone who has looked at it as alive but in slow decline.

It is worth the stop anyway, and arguably it is a better stop than it was. A cedar this size takes a millennium to build and one night of weather to halve, and here you can see both facts at the same time: the intact side going up, the wreckage of the other side where it fell.

The Big Cedar trail leaves a signed pull-off on Highway 101 between Ruby Beach and Kalaloch. It is a few hundred feet, flat, and free with the park. Read the signs when you get there. The 2014 damage is the reason they exist.

name: El Palo Alto

location.address: El Palo Alto Park, on the banks of San Francisquito Creek near Alma Street, Palo Alto, California
location.neighbourhood: El Palo Alto Park, next to the Caltrain tracks where they cross Alma Street

access: Free, public park, visible and reachable at any time.
transport: Adjacent to the Palo Alto Caltrain corridor; walkable from downtown Palo Alto and University Ave Caltrain station.
story:
Palo Alto is named for how tall this redwood used to be. El Palo Alto is Spanish for the tall stick, the tree is on the city seal, and since 1930 it has lost about sixteen metres off the top.

It measured 162 feet then. It stands at roughly 110 today, about thirty three and a half metres, with a dead top. The cause was not a storm or a disease but plumbing: the water table under San Francisquito Creek was drawn down between 1865 and 1955, and the crown died back progressively as the water went.

The tree is old enough for all of that to be a late chapter. Estimates put it at a thousand years and a little beyond, which means it was already several centuries into its life when a Spanish expedition is recorded camping at this creek in 1769.

It may now be the most closely monitored tree in California. A donated assessment in March 2025 ran ground-penetrating radar under it, excavated the roots with compressed air, flew a drone through the crown and left a prism on the trunk to track whether it moves. The verdict was decay and a dead top, on sound buttress roots.

It stands in El Palo Alto Park on the creek bank by Alma Street, walkable from downtown, with Caltrain going past a few metres away. A survivor rather than a giant, which is the more interesting of the two.

name: General Sherman Tree

location.address: Giant Forest, Sequoia National Park, Tulare County, California
location.neighbourhood: Giant Forest, on the Main Trail, about 0.5 miles from the Wolverton/Sherman Tree parking lot

access: Paid entry (Sequoia National Park entrance fee); a short, partly paved, downhill walk from the main parking lot (uphill on the return, or use the seasonal shuttle).
transport: No public transit; the nearest town is Three Rivers, CA, about 45 minutes' drive from the park entrance.
story:
In September 2021, with the KNP Complex Fire burning into the Giant Forest, park staff wrapped the base of this tree in aluminium foil. It worked. The fire came through the grove and the tree was unharmed.

That is roughly the class of trouble a sequoia is built for. This one holds about 1,487 cubic metres of trunk, which makes it the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth, and the number doing the work is girth rather than height. At 83.6 metres it is a fairly ordinary tall sequoia. At about 31 metres round the base it is not.

Its age is genuinely unsettled. Most estimates land between 2,300 and 2,700 years, older ones ran as high as 3,200, and nobody is going to core it to settle the argument, so both figures stay on this page.

It stands on the Main Trail in the Giant Forest, about half a mile from the Sherman Tree parking lot. The walk down is short and part paved; the walk back is the uphill half, and a seasonal shuttle runs for anyone who would rather not. Sequoia National Park charges at the gate. Once you are through it, the most famous tree in the country costs nothing to stand in front of.

name: The Pinchot Sycamore

location.address: Pinchot Sycamore Park, Route 185 (Hopmeadow St / Simsbury Rd) on the east bank of the Farmington River, Simsbury, CT
location.neighbourhood: Simsbury, near the base of Talcott Mountain

access: Free, public town park (Pinchot Sycamore Park), open grounds with a boat launch onto the Farmington River; floodlit at night since a 1997 lighting project.
transport: No direct public transit found; car access off Route 185 south of Simsbury town center. Nearest published city is Boston or New York, both well over an hour away by road; treat as its own place (Simsbury, CT).
story:
This sycamore is considerably wider than it is tall: about thirty metres up, and an average spread of forty three metres across. Connecticut has nothing bigger, and the national register lists it as the champion of its species.

It was measured again in November 2025 at 884 centimetres round, a trunk that takes five or six people holding hands to enclose. It is doing this on the flood plain of the Farmington River, which is exactly the wet ground an American sycamore wants. Its age is given as over two hundred years and possibly beyond three hundred. There is no planting date, and nobody has cored it.

It carries the name of Gifford Pinchot, the conservationist who later governed Connecticut, which makes it one of the few champion trees named for someone who would have known what the title meant.

The town built a park around it rather than the other way round: open lawn, a boat launch onto the river, and floodlights since 1997, so the frame is legible after dark as well. The October snowstorm of 2011 took some of the canopy and left the heavy lower limbs alone, which is why the shape survived intact.

Free, open, on Route 185 south of the village centre.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the white upper limbs show

name: The Sunderland Buttonball Tree
age_estimate: well over 350 years, possibly closer to 400
access: Free, stands on a public street (North Main Street) in the town center; a commemorative plaque was installed in front of it in 1987.
transport: No public transit found; roadside in Sunderland town center, car access. Roughly 15 km / 25 minutes by road north of Amherst; not close to any city on our published US list (nearest are Boston/New York, both 2+ hours). Treat as its own place (Sunderland, MA).
story:
The plaque at its foot dates the tree against the US Constitution. It was already standing, and already large, when the document was signed in 1787.

Tradition has it seeded before 1665, which puts it well over three hundred and fifty years old and by some accounts near four hundred. That is tradition rather than a count of rings, and it is worth saying so, but the measurements are consistent with an old tree: 782 centimetres round at chest height when it was last measured in 2019, over thirty four metres tall, with a crown spreading forty three metres. It is widely called the largest tree in Massachusetts. The local line goes further and calls it the widest tree this side of the Mississippi, which is a saying rather than a survey.

Buttonball is the New England name for the American sycamore, and it comes from the seed balls that hang on the bare limbs through the winter before breaking apart in spring.

There is no gate, no ticket and no path to find. It stands on the verge of North Main Street in the middle of the village, so you park, walk over and put a hand on the bark. The commemorative plaque went in beside it in 1987, roughly three hundred and twenty years into the tree's life.

best_time.label: December and January, when the seed balls that give it its name hang on bare limbs

name: Octopus Tree

location.address: Cape Meares State Scenic Viewpoint, near Cape Meares Lighthouse, Tillamook County, Oregon
location.neighbourhood: a short walk from the Cape Meares Lighthouse parking area

access: Free, Oregon State Parks scenic viewpoint; short, easy, well-marked walk from the lighthouse parking area.
transport: No public transit; nearest town is Tillamook, OR, about a 20 to 25 minute drive.
story:
This spruce has no trunk. Six heavy limbs leave a base roughly fifteen metres wide, run out sideways for as much as five metres, and only then turn and climb, so the tree reads as six trees that agreed on a starting point.

How it got that way is an open argument. Local tradition holds that Native people shaped the young tree deliberately, and one version of the story says the limbs were meant to cradle canoes in burial rites. That account is disputed and has never been confirmed. The tree is worth the walk under either explanation.

It is roughly two hundred and fifty to three hundred years old and over fourteen metres round the base, and it has collected names in proportion: the Octopus Tree, the Candelabra Tree, the Council Tree and, from someone less taken with it, the Monstrosity Tree. Oregon lists it as a Heritage Tree.

It stands a few minutes' walk from the Cape Meares Lighthouse parking area at the Cape Meares State Scenic Viewpoint, out on the headland about twenty minutes west of Tillamook. The path is short, easy and signed, and none of it costs anything.
